The Northern broad-footed mole (Scapanus latimanus) exhibits a basal metabolic rate that aligns with its fossorial lifestyle and modest body size. Respirometry trials conducted under controlled laboratory conditions, at a body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], have measured a maximum resting oxygen consumption of approximately 76.3 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 76.3 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic rate is relatively elevated compared to surface-dwelling insectivores of similar mass, a pattern often attributed to the high energetic costs of burrowing through compacted soil. The energy demands of constant subterranean excavation, combined with the thermoregulatory challenges of a stable but cool microclimate, likely drive this elevated expenditure. Such physiological measurements provide critical context for understanding the energetic budget of this talpid, linking its metabolic capacity to its daily activity patterns and foraging requirements in the patchy, prey-rich soils of its California and Oregon range.

Reproductive output in Scapanus latimanus is modest, reflecting a life-history strategy common among small, energetically constrained subterranean mammals. Females typically give birth to a single annual litter, with litter sizes ranging from 3 to 4 pups [N_R_i = 3 to 4 pups]. This reproductive event occurs once per year [F_R_i = once per year], constrained by the lengthy gestation and extended period of maternal care required for altricial neonates. The timing of parturition is likely synchronized with peak soil invertebrate abundance in the spring. At birth, the altricial pups are extremely small, with an estimated wet weight of only 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams]. This birth mass is based on data from the congeneric Scapanus townsendii and is consistent with the general pattern among moles, where neonates are highly underdeveloped relative to adult dimensions, requiring intensive lactation and burrow-bound nursing.

Juveniles undergo a rapid, though extended, period of growth within the maternal burrow system, dependent entirely on milk. The weaning period, marking the transition to nutritional independence, occurs at approximately 40 days after birth [tx = approximately 40 days after birth] when the pups begin to consume soil at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] invertebrates. The timing of this nutritional emancipation is closely tied to the regulated temperature of the nest chamber, typically maintained at around 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. By the time suckling ceases, the juvenile moles have achieved a substantial portion of their growth, with a wet weight at weaning of roughly 40 grams [Wwx = roughly 40 grams]. This represents a significant gain from the 5-gram birth mass, reflecting the high energetic value of mole milk, which is rich in lipids and proteins necessary for rapid somatic development in a thermally stable but food-limited environment.

Full adult body size, or the ultimate wet weight, in Scapanus latimanus is reached after several months of independent foraging and is recorded at approximately 61 grams [Wwi = approximately 61 grams]. The trajectory from the approximate 40 gram weaning mass to this adult asymptote is characterized by an intensive period of soil excavation and prey capture. Sexual maturation, defined by the onset of puberty, is a comparatively slow process for a mammal of this size. Data from the related species Scapanus orarius suggest that this species does not become reproductively mature until approximately 300 days after birth [tp = approximately 300 days after birth] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This delayed maturation at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] likely reflects the considerable time required to develop the robust skeletal and muscular anatomy necessary for efficient burrowing before any energy can be allocated to reproductive tissues.

Longevity records for fossorial mammals are often challenging to obtain, but data for Scapanus latimanus, extrapolated from the closely related Scapanus orarius, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. When maintained under captive conditions at a stable body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the gestation period associated with this reproductive cycle is remarkably short for an insectivore of this size, lasting only 28 days [tg = 28 days]. This abbreviated gestation is typical of talpids and results in the birth of extremely altricial pups. The protracted postnatal development reflects the challenges of fossorial life, where juveniles must develop the musculature and digging skills necessary to secure their own territories before reproduction becomes possible.
